title: 8 short thoughts about 'Back to Basics.'
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Responding to an Economist education special, Skelton lays out eight short thoughts on the slogan back to basics. He accepts that basics matter and that most teachers have not abandoned them, but asks whose basics are meant, since people differ on what they are. He argues the phrase often works like a political slogan that hides restrictive agendas: a knowledge-only curriculum, a narrow focus on literacy and maths, telling-style teaching, cost saving, or curriculum reduction. He thinks a full curriculum is a genuine problem that needs focus, but not at the expense of breadth. He closes by stating the entitlements every student should have and says he will wear the badge only if it does not narrow experience.
points: The slogan back to basics is easy to agree with, so it can conceal contested choices about knowledge versus skills, teaching method and cost.
Skelton doubts that schools have deliberately left basics behind, and suggests any problem is more systemic than a matter of teacher mindset.
Knowledge alone cannot define the basics, because students become scientists or writers by developing skills as well as learning facts.
Overfull curricula are a real issue, but reducing student access to a wide range of subjects is the wrong remedy.
Every student should meet a basic range of subjects, and those weaker at maths and literacy must have subjects in which they can shine.
quotes: Unless our learners are extraordinarily talented or gifted, it seems impossible for most of us to get better at anything without starting with the basics. The basics are the foundations on which everything else is built. Let’s at least start by acknowledging that the basics matter.

In my experience in tens of schools and hundreds of classrooms, I don’t think we have left the ‘basics’ behind, at least not deliberately. I don’t see most teachers knowingly disabling their students from paying enough attention to the basics.
One of the big issues with ‘back to basics’ is that we all have a different view of what the basics might be and that depends partly on what we want our students to become.

Used well, it, too, could be the basis for a complex discussion of what needs to happen in education and schooling. But used badly - and it is mostly used badly - it is a cover up for restrictive learning and teaching experiences.

That’s why one of the most important questions is to ask ‘Do we want our students to learn science facts or learn how to be scientists?’ The answer for many people is that we want both and both involves knowledge and skills.

Skills learning often requires laboratories, workshops, pools and theatres which require funding and are relatively expensive when compared to knowledge lessons. Advocating a ‘back to basics’ approach can often be a financial decision hiding behind an apparent educational argument.

We do have to do something to make our curricula more manageable. That may well be focusing on the basics of what matters at different ages and stages. What can’t be right is to solve the problem by restricting student access to a wide variety of subjects.
